summary: Coos County fire-tower site on a 1,673-foot summit listed under Berlin; listed as gone, and no source read describes the site today.

facts.status_note: Listed as gone; no source read describes what remains at the site today

staffing.status: staffed only in high-risk periods (class description; Lonesome Ridge named as an example)

evidence.supports: In Coos County; listed as Tower Gone
Secondary lookouts were on less prominent peaks and staffed only in high-risk periods
evidence.quote: Secondary Lookouts were on less prominent peaks, with shorter views, and staffed only during high risk periods.

evidence.supports: Lonesome Ridge named as an example of a secondary lookout
evidence.quote: Examples are Lonesome Ridge, Osceola and West Royce.

evidence.supports: 1910 system of fire towers in the White Mountains
evidence.quote: In 1910 the NH Timberland Owners Association, the state of New Hampshire, and the US Forest Service worked together to produce a system of fire towers in the White Mountains.

evidence.supports: A large number of New Hampshire towers destroyed in the 1938 hurricane
evidence.quote: A large number of the towers were destroyed in the 1938 hurricane

evidence.supports: A video is titled as showing the tower's remains; contents not read

notes_for_editor: Thin record: no built date, builder, fire, or removal date could be verified from a page I could quote. A Berlin history post on Facebook (facebook.com/berlinnhhistory, post 1464385156984315) says the tower was erected in 1936 and abandoned around 1940, and says Berlin had two towers within city limits (the other on Deer Mountain). That post's text is not readable through the cached reader, so it is not quoted or used. Check it by hand and, if confirmed, find a second source before adding a built event. The NH Family Hikes elevation list is the only source for the 1,673-foot figure. The YouTube video may describe what remains; its contents were not readable.
